Seeing monitor · simulator output

Polaris through a 50 mm aperture

At this size the star is almost a perfect Airy pattern, and the atmosphere moves it around. The monitor measures that motion at 88 frames per second. Everything here comes from the simulator's wave-optics code, not from a sky.

Image at 4× finer sampling

The same 2 ms exposure, 0.48″ per pixel, with the diffraction rings.

What the camera records

Bin1 pixels of 1.91″, with photon and read noise. The ring marks the measured centroid.

time0.000 s x+0.00″ y+0.00″ frame1 / 240

What the camera measures

Each frame gives one centroid. Over a few seconds the centroids trace the image motion. Its root mean square is what the monitor turns into seeing.

Image motion over time

Centroid offset along each sensor axis, one point per frame. The dashed lines mark one standard deviation from the theory.

xytheory ±1σ

Where the star lands

All frames at once. The dashed circle is the theory's one-sigma radius per axis.

Motion spectrum

Power of the centroid at 1 kHz sampling. An 88 fps camera sees only the part left of the dotted line.

selected seeingthe other two

Exposure time

A longer exposure averages the motion and lowers the measured variance. This is why fast mode uses 2 ms.

The simulator against theory

Root mean square image motion per axis for a 50 mm aperture, in arcseconds. The simulated column averages 2 ms exposures over about 200 s of simulated sky, so its sampling error is a few percent.

Frozen flow in slow motion

Wind carries the same wavefront across the aperture. Here the instants are 0.25 ms apart and the playback is slowed 200 times. The camera would take one sample every 11 ms.

Tilt

Image motion in this 30 ms stretch.

The pictures use the simulator's own turbulence model and wave-optics renderer, so the numbers above are measurements of that code. Polaris is rendered at 8,650 electrons per millisecond, a research-notes estimate good to ±30%, with Poisson noise and 2.65 electrons of read noise. The simulator is still being validated, so treat this page as a snapshot.
